title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance (Unified)
author: Daniel Kim
content:
Summary:
This document consolidates Redwood Inference's cross-cutting architecture and engineering standards for API design, coding practices, infrastructure (IaC and deployment), model-serving, observability, and performance. It includes a recorded architectural decision (ADR) about API contract conventions and a rollout checklist for teams adopting these standards.

Audience:
- Software engineers and ML engineers building services that will run on Redwood Hosted, Dedicated, or Private deployments.
- Platform and SRE teams responsible for service onboarding, SLIs/SLOs, and operational readiness.

Goals:
1. Provide a single reference for norms to increase interoperability, reduce operational toil, and improve reliability and performance across services.
2. Make API contracts predictable and versionable so clients and downstream systems can evolve independently.
3. Ensure observability and performance requirements are captured at design time to avoid late-stage incidents.

Applies to:
- Any new microservice, model-serving endpoint, or SDK surface developed after 2025-12-01.
- Existing services should migrate according to the Migration Plan section.

1) API Standards
- Spec-first: All externally consumable endpoints must ship with an OpenAPI 3.1 specification checked into the service repo under /openapi/openapi.yaml. Use the company OpenAPI generator for SDKs and mocks.
- Versioning and compatibility:
  - URL versioning: /v1/, /v2/ only for breaking changes. Prefer additive, non-breaking changes within minor versions.
  - Backwards compatibility: Maintain previous minor/major versions for at least 90 days or per product SLA.
- Authentication/Authorization:
  - Use bearer tokens (JWT) issued by Redwood Identity for internal services; OAuth2 for external integrations.
  - Route-level RBAC metadata must be declared in the OpenAPI extensions (x-rbac-role).
- Error model:
  - Standard error envelope: {"error": {"code": string, "message": string, "details": optional object}}
  - Use 4xx for client errors and 5xx for server errors; include machine-readable error codes (kebab-case).
- Pagination, Filtering and Sorting:
  - Cursor-based pagination required for list endpoints returning > 100 items.
  - Use query parameters for filters and sorting; document allowed fields in the spec.
- Rate limiting and quotas:
  - Endpoint-level rate limit headers: X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset.

2) Coding Standards
- Languages and frameworks:
  - Backend default: Go (1.20+) for latency-sensitive services, Python (3.11+) for data pipelines and evaluation harnesses, TypeScript (Node 18+) for web-facing admin services.
- Formatting and linting:
  - Enforce gofmt/golangci-lint for Go, black/ruff/pyright for Python, eslint/prettier for TypeScript. CI must run linters and fail on errors.
- Types and contracts:
  - Schema generation from OpenAPI or Protobufs is preferred. Avoid handwritten client models where codegen is available.
- Testing:
  - Unit test coverage: teams must target a minimum of 60% line coverage for new services. Critical paths (auth, input validation, model pre/post-processing) must include property-based or fuzz tests.
- Dependency policy:
  - Regular dependency scans (Snyk or internal scanner) and quarterly dependency update sprints. No unreviewed native binary deps; approve via security team if required.

3) Infrastructure Standards
- IaC and repositories:
  - Use Terraform as canonical IaC; modules live in infra-modules repo. All environment-specific values must be in per-account variable files, not in source code.
- Environments and accounts:
  - Clear separation: prod, staging, dev. Network ACLs and IAM policies must follow least privilege.
- Secrets and keys:
  - Use KMS-backed secrets (HashiCorp Vault or cloud KMS) and avoid embedding secrets in images or repo.
- CI/CD and rollouts:
  - Must support canary or progressive rollouts with automated rollback on error thresholds. CD pipelines must require a review and pass automated integration tests.
- Capacity and autoscaling:
  - Define autoscaling SLOs for CPU/GPU-backed fleets. Default scaling policy: target 60% utilization with headroom for 2x burst.

4) Model-Serving Standards
- Model versioning and artifacts:
  - Every model artifact must be immutable and referenced by digest (sha256). Model metadata includes: model_id, version, backend (ONNX/Torch/Triton/grpc), quantization_profile, tokenizer_hash, and evaluation_summary_link.
- Runtime and container images:
  - Use curated runtime base images maintained by eng-serving-runtime team. Images must be scanned and pinned.
- Latency and batching policies:
  - Default per-request latency SLOs vary by profile (see Performance section). Batching configurations must be declared in the model manifest with max_batch_size and preferred_latency_target_ms.
- Fallbacks and graceful degradation:
  - Services must declare compatible fallback model variants in the manifest. Smart routing will prefer lower-cost quantized variants if they meet quality thresholds.
- A/B and rollout:
  - Model rollouts use traffic-splitting and quality monitors. All rollouts require a preflight evaluation suite and monitoring hooks.

5) Observability Standards
- Tracing:
  - Distributed tracing is mandatory for request paths crossing service boundaries. Use OpenTelemetry and propagate tracecontext headers.
- Metrics:
  - Exported metrics must use the Prometheus exposition format and include these baseline metrics: request_count, request_latency_ms (histogram), error_count, queue_size, batch_size, model_kv_cache_hit_rate.
- Logs:
  - Structured JSON logs (timestamp, level, service, trace_id, span_id, request_id). Avoid PII in logs; scrub inputs for customer-sensitive fields.
- Dashboards and alerts:
  - Every service must ship at least one production dashboard (latency, error rate, throughput, capacity). Alerting thresholds should be tied to SLO burn rate and actionable runbooks.

6) Performance Standards
- SLO taxonomy (examples):
  - API generation endpoints: p95 latency <= 350ms (small responses), p99 <= 800ms.
  - Embeddings endpoints: p95 <= 120ms, p99 <= 350ms.
  - Model streaming endpoints: tail p99 <= 1.5s per chunk.
- Load testing:
  - Services must run load tests that simulate realistic traffic (sequence length distributions, concurrency mix). Results and runbooks must be committed alongside the service.
- Capacity planning:
  - SRE maintains fleet capacity targets. Services must provide cost-per-token and expected traffic profile for capacity modeling.

7) Decision Record (ADR): API Contract & Spec-First Policy (ADR-2026-03)
- Status: accepted
- Decision drivers:
  1. Need for consistent SDK generation and mock servers.
  2. Reduce client integration bugs from implicit contract drift.
  3. Support for telemetry, role metadata, and contract evolution.
- Considered alternatives:
  A) Ad-hoc hand-written API docs and client libraries.
  B) GraphQL-first approach.
  C) OpenAPI spec-first with company extensions (chosen).
- Decision: We adopt OpenAPI 3.1 as the canonical API contract format for all external and internal HTTP services. Small, latency-sensitive RPCs may still use gRPC with proto files; in those cases a generated OpenAPI facade must be provided for web clients.
- Consequences:
  - Pros: standardization enables automated SDKs, contract tests, and consistent validation.
  - Cons: additional discipline on teams to maintain the spec; initial effort to migrate legacy services.

8) Migration & Rollout Plan
1. New services: adopt these standards immediately. PR templates and repo templates have been updated.
2. Legacy services: teams to create a migration plan within 90 days. Prioritization will be based on traffic and business criticality.
3. Platform support: eng-developer-experience will provide OpenAPI scaffolding, linters, and a spec-validator GitHub Action.

9) Ownership and Governance
- Standards owner: Architecture & Standards council (chairs: Daniel Kim, Priya Shah).
- Exceptions: Exceptions can be requested via the standards-exceptions RFC process and require documented risk mitigation and approval from the council.

10) Appendix: Checklist for Service Onboarding
- [ ] OpenAPI spec checked in and validated.
- [ ] Linting and unit tests passing in CI.
- [ ] Prometheus metrics and OpenTelemetry tracing added.
- [ ] Production dashboard created and alerting rules configured.
- [ ] Model manifest (if applicable) includes digest, quantization profile, and fallback variants.
- [ ] Load test results and capacity notes checked in.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)
Q: When should a team use gRPC vs. HTTP+OpenAPI?
A: Use gRPC for high-throughput, low-latency internal RPCs where client platforms support it. Provide an OpenAPI facade for browser/third-party consumption.

Q: How are breaking changes communicated?
A: Breaking changes must be announced on the arch-standards mailing list and a migration plan posted in the service docs. Maintain previous major version for at least 90 days or as required by customers.

Feedback and updates:
Please send feedback or propose revisions via the architecture-standards GitHub repo or contact the council chairs. This document will be reviewed quarterly or on major platform changes.
